content.title: Spotting Physical Access and Security Scams
content.summary: Learn how to spot and defend against fraudulent emails impersonating building access and physical security alerts.
content.body_markdown:
We all get tricked sometimes, especially when an email looks like an official alert about building passes, office badge updates, or physical security systems [ORG]. In Sales, fast responses are key, but scammers count on urgency to bypass our guardrails [S4].

## What is happening

Cybercriminals frequently send emails impersonating office management, security teams, or facility administrators [S4]. These messages claim that your physical access badge has expired, a building security system requires urgent identity verification, or visitor logging procedures have changed [S3, S4]. Scammers use these realistic scenarios to trick you into clicking malicious links or submitting corporate credentials on fake login portals [S2, S3].

In our Nebulon telemetry, physical access notifications have been a challenging spot for our team, with 8 out of 8 simulated physical access emails missed [ORG]. Scammers know we want to keep office entry smooth, so they create fake emergencies to rush our decisions before we have time to check if the request is real [S4].

## 3 Red flags to watch out for

- **Urgent requests to retain access:** Messages claiming your physical building access, badge, or facility pass will be deactivated immediately unless you click a link or re-enter credentials [S3, S4].
- **Unusual login links or shortened URLs:** Web links directing you to external, non-standard websites rather than Nebulon's official secure portals [S4].
- **Unverified contacts asking for credentials or remote access:** Requests claiming to be technical or facility assistance demanding password confirmation, identity verification, or software installation [S1, S6].

## What to do

If you receive an unexpected notification regarding building badges, physical security updates, or facility access:

- **Pause and verify:** Never rush when a message creates a sense of urgency [S4]. Take a moment to inspect the sender details.
- **Use a second channel:** Verify any unexpected security or badge request by contacting the facility or security team directly using known, official channels rather than clicking email links [S7].
- **Check URLs:** Ensure any website you log into uses a secure connection starting with `https://` on an official company domain [S2, S4].
- **Avoid downloading unauthorized apps:** Do not grant remote access or download applications received via email links or chat messages [S1, S6].

## How to report

If you spot a suspicious building access alert or any unexpected physical security scam email, do not click any links or attachments [S1]. Forward the message immediately to **security@nebulon.example.com** [ORG]. Reporting suspicious emails protects the entire team and keeps our workplaces safe!

Urgency and fake emergencies are designed to make you act without checking.
Always verify physical access requests through a trusted secondary channel.
Report suspicious emails promptly to security@nebulon.example.com.

### Secure Yourself & Your Family

We can all protect ourselves, our friends and our families from online threats. It’s fast. It’s easy.

### Use Strong Passwords

Using strong passwords and a password manager are some easy ways to protect ourselves from someone logging into an account and stealing data or money.

### Turn on MFA

Multifactor authentication means using more than a password to access an app or account. With MFA, we might be asked to enter a text code or use a fingerprint. It alerts us and prevents others from accessing our accounts.
